question: How do I make amends for wronging people in my youth whom I can no longer find?
asked: She is now an elderly lady in her sixties and, looking back, feels she wronged specific people in her youth. She has repented for the wrong, but those people are no longer part of her life; she cannot locate them and doesn't know their current status. How can she make up for the wrong she did to them?
answer:
This again is a very, very good question. It shows, inshallah ta'ala, that our sister is genuinely repenting to Allah. She is feeling guilty about whatever she has done. We do not know, but again, the point is that it's generic for all of us. We've all done things to people that we should not have done. And some of those people are still in our lives, and some of them are no longer in our lives, either through death or, in this case, literally it's been, what, 30, 40 years, and she has no clue where they are. She might have said something or done something; we've all been there. So now she is asking what can be done. And this is a very good question, and in fact it shows a sincere desire.

Our Prophet ﷺ said that whoever has done dhulm to his brother, whether it is regarding his honor or by taking his property, which he should not have done, let him resolve that dhulm before the day comes when there shall be no gold and silver, but rather there shall only be good deeds. And the good deeds will be given in accordance with the amount of dhulm that he has done, and so the person will continue to give his good deeds. And if he runs out of good deeds, then the other person's bad deeds will be transferred to the first person. The hadith is in Bukhari and Muslim.

This is a very terrifying hadith, because what it shows is that on the Day of Judgment, those people who have done wrong shall be held accountable by Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala, and they will have to make up for the wrong that they have done. And that's why our Prophet ﷺ said: get rid of any wrongdoings, make them halal, in this world before the next world. So every single one of us should think long and hard: who have I unintentionally hurt? Who have I done something to, such that they might be able to say something against me on the Day of Judgment? And once that person comes to our mind, if they're in our lives and they're still alive, we should go to them now.

What can we do if we go to them? The best thing to do, and the safest thing to do, is to literally come up to them and apologize and say, "My dearest brother or sister in Islam, I did something I shouldn't have done. Can you forgive me for the sake of Allah? And Allah will reward you for that forgiveness." And that's the ideal. And of course, why should the other brother do it? Because he wants Allah's reward: when he forgives, Allah will forgive him. And he might put a condition, if he knows what you've done. He might say, "Look, you said some things about me; you need to go and correct what you said," or, "You did this and that." So he might put a reasonable condition, and then you should fulfill that condition if it is reasonable and pertinent to what you have done. That's if you have direct access.

Our sister says she no longer has access. What do you do? Another scenario: you might have access, but the person doesn't know, and if you were to inform the person, it would actually be even more problematic. It would bring a whole scenario of "Oh my God, why did you do this and this?" and it might even make the situation worse. Suppose a few years have passed, and you said something that was backbiting, and you shouldn't have done that, or something even worse, and the person doesn't know and things are fine. If you were to go and tell them, you are worried your friendship, your brotherhood or sisterhood, will be broken, and you want to make up. So, both of these scenarios: number one, you don't know where the person is; and number two, you don't want to inform the person because it's going to make matters worse. There are a number of things that you can do.

The first thing you can do is guesstimate a monetary value for the damage that you have done, given the gravity of your crime and also the amount of money that you have. Because the person who has a million dollars and the person who has ten thousand dollars, it's not the same if they each give one hundred dollars. You know what's going to pinch you, and that's going to be equivalent to the amount of harm that you've done. So, given the harm that you've done and given your socio-economic status, put the two together and make it in your own mind, because you have to answer to Allah. You are being your own judge, jury and executioner in this regard. You have to give enough that you can say to Allah, with a clear conscience on the Day of Judgment, "O Allah, I did such and such, and I know I did wrong, so I have given $100 in sadaqah for the reward to go to him, so that I'm not going to get the $100, but the harm that I have done is going to be equalized by this $100." Now again, you will set the price, because you know. In your own mind, roughly make an estimate: "I think this much hasanat of a hundred dollars will be worth the damage of my sayyi'at." So then you've counterbalanced it, and then you give that charity. That's one thing that you can do.

Now, by the way, this is assuming that you have backbitten him or something like that. If you have actually stolen some money, or you have something in your possession that you should not have, in this case you must get rid of it. It's not yours; you took it incorrectly, and you give it to charity. So if you are physically in possession of an item, in ownership of an item, through dhulm, then you need to get rid of that item because it is not yours, and expect the reward to go to the person. But you still have to do more, because that wasn't your item in the first place; you took it. I'm just giving an example. So, as we said, you give a financial penalty: on top of getting rid of that item for charity, if you have it, you have to give your own charity from your own wealth. Pinch yourself: "Hey, I shouldn't have done that, and this is for his sake." That's the second thing you can do.

The third thing you can do is to make du'a for that person. Make du'a for that person. Raise your hands up to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala and say, "O Allah, bless him with more money. O Allah, forgive his sins. O Allah, give him a good family," whatever it might be. And continue to make du'a until you feel that you have done enough to make up for the harm that you did. And once again, you yourself will be judge, jury and executioner. You will take into account yourself how much damage you've done, and then say, "You know what, that means I should make du'a for him at least 50 times." So whatever I've done, at least 50 times I'm going to raise my hands and, by name, thinking of him, make du'a sincerely. So that on the Day of Judgment, this person will come, and he will see the wrong that you've done, and he will see all of the du'a, and your du'a will be more than the wrong. He can't say anything. He cannot say anything. He says, "Look, he has made up for it," in the eyes of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala.

And then the last thing that you can do is sincerely, sincerely raise your hands to Allah and ask His forgiveness as well, because you have also wronged yourself in the eyes of Allah by doing something you should not have done. So if you are sincere and you genuinely turn to Allah for forgiveness, and you have returned an item that you took unjustly or given it away, and you give a financial penalty that you think is enough, and you make du'a for the person, then **inshallah ta'ala, all of this put together will free you from any liability on the Day of Judgment, if you are sincere.** And Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala knows best.
